utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I gather, Mr. Ivetic, that you will be leading the next witness, who is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. That will be Professor Dr. Zoran Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning again, Dr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, could you please first tell us your full name, first and last, and tell us briefly about your background and occupation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Stankovic. I was born on the 9th of November, 1954, in the village of Tegoviste, municipality of Vladicin Han. I'm a physician by profession. I'm a specialist in forensic medicine. From the very outset of my career, I served in the military first as head of the garrison infirmary in Pec; then I was a forensic doctor in the Institute For Pathology And Forensic Medicine of the Military Medical Academy; and later on from 2002 until 2005, I was head of the Military Medical Academy. I am a major-general, retired. During the course of my professional career, I lectured in King's College at Cambridge and then in several countries such as the Ukraine. I was also in The Hague and Amsterdam and Utrecht. After that, I published about 60 scientific and professional papers. I took part in the writing of four or five books. I was an expert witness in The Hague Tribunal in General Krstic's case. Also, inter alia, I was a member of the commission of the Government of Yugoslavia, the truth commission of the ad hoc group of Vukovar, and I am a permanent forensic expert for Serbia and Republika Srpska, and I also testified at the higher court in Thessaloniki.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could call up Exhibit 6D 711 on the monitors in e-court, sir, I would ask you to take a look at this and tell us if this document is your curriculum vitae and if there are any additions or supplements that need to be made to the same to complete it. I think you've done that in answer to the first question already.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the text is in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You should have the text in the Serbian on the left side of the screen about now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just have to say that currently I teach forensic medicine at the Faculty Of Dental Medicine in Pancevo, and also I teach in Belgrade at the police academy, and from October 2005 until the 15th of May, 2007, I was minister of defence of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro, later on the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you please enlighten us on the precise topic and subject matter that was examined by you and defended as part of your doctoral dissertation as part of your studies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: My doctorate has to do with dealing with corpses in wartime and it is entitled, Problems Of Examining Corpses In Conditions Of War. I examined 1.360 cases and several variables in terms of all the problems cropping up in relation to corpses. Some of these problems and dilemmas will be the subject of my expertise today in view of the findings that are in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now just to get some specifics, you indicated that you are at the dental college and the police criminalistic academy. Could you tell us what courses or responsibilities you have at those institutions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are lectures that primarily have to do with forensic medicine, that is to say the application of medicine or the explanation of all the medical concepts that are of importance for court proceedings. Primarily, this pertains to the classification and qualification of body injuries, causes of death, and all injuries that involve violence, poisoning; at the same time, autopsies, bodies, and all activities related to forensic medicine. I have to say that Serbia is one of the few countries that has forensic medicine as an isolated subject, like in Great Britain. In contrast to that, in the United States it is called a court pathologist or something like that. However, the activities are the same, those of a court pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned lecturing at the Kings College, and indeed, in your CV it mentions the Kings College at Cambridge in Great Britain. Could you tell us what was the precise nature of the lectures that you presented at the Kings College at Cambridge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I carried out autopsies of about 5.000 corpses, so practically this involved all the big mass graves that were dealt with at the time during the war operations. I can say now that I worked in several cities like Vukovar, Siroko, Kula, Nevesinje, Trebinje, Bilaca, Sarajevo, Bratunac, all of Eastern Bosnia, in fact; then Mrkonjic Grad, Banja Luka; in Kosovo Klina and Lake Radonjic where I was in attendance. Since I participated and led so many activities in relation to mass graves, then I was invited to give lectures on victims of war at all of these institutions, as you've seen, including Kings College at Cambridge and the British parliament and in the Ukraine too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor Stankovic, could you please tell us if you have testified as an expert in any legal proceedings domestically in Serbia or the former Yugoslavia and if said testimony was exclusively on the side of defendants, or have you had occasion to testify for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, practically every day I take part in such court proceedings that have to do with violence, and I give my forensic opinion. I would particularly like to highlight as far as this Tribunal is concerned, at least, that I took part in providing expert opinions regarding victims from Kosovo. It had to do with the processing of the well near Klina in Kosovo. The trial was before the district court in Kraljevo, and that is where I presented my findings and opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Doctor, you've mentioned all the experience that you've had dealing with mass or multiple graves arising out of wartime situations. Based upon your knowledge, training, experience, and area of expertise within the forensic sciences, are there any nuances or peculiarities relating to applying forensic science to the examination of so-called mass graves that differs from normal, everyday forensic science work that most professionals in your field are exposed to, that is to say examination of single or small number of corpses in clinical circumstances. That is to say, would you consider the examination of mass graves to be a specialised area of forensic medical science, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In order for someone to deal with a mass grave, in addition to theoretical experience he must have practical experience. In day-to-day work, there are numerous problems that crop up and that you have to resolve, regardless of how high level of training you have had if you did not see what projectile wounds look like or, for example, if you did not see how mine and explosive devices actually work, you cannot be a proper expert in this field until you see things like that. For example, if you look at a 556 bullet, it has a very characteristic entry wound. Sometimes it is barely perceptible as opposed to the exit wound that is very big. Then, the experience we had when we were in Vukovar. Eight of our soldiers got killed in Vukovar, and 24 lost one or both legs at the moment when we were walking up to the corpses that were there and when we were gathering them for forensic examination. When we realized that they had been mined, then we realized that the site had to be dealt with in a completely different way. Also, when we were involved in exhumations of the mass grave in Rogatica. At that moment, the son who saw his father and recognised him by his footwear, in -- at that moment he tried to dig his father's body out as past as possible, and he lost his own foot because there was a booby-trap there. So this is the kind of experience that one can gain only when war operations are actually going on, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, Professor Stankovic, did you have an occasion to prepare a written report specifically in professional analysis on behalf of all the Defence teams in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I provided my findings and my opinion that were submitted to the Tribunal. At the same time, it is actually -- could I just have a moment, please. It involves 13 pages with 19 conclusions related to Kotlina and nine related -- nine conclusions related to Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please take a moment to call up Exhibit 6D 670 on e-court. And, sir, when this document comes up, I would ask you to take a look at the same and tell me whether you -- this is the professional work product or analysis that you prepared based on your knowledge and expertise relating to the matters of relevance for these instant court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you please take a moment to highlight for us the materials which you had occasion to review and analyse for purposes of preparing this report and performing your preparations for testifying as an expert before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the material, I reviewed the report of the Federal Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Austria. They worked in Kotlina in 1999, then the collective report of the French forensic mission of Kosovo in the summer of 1999. I also saw the recordings of Dr. Liri Loshi; the forensic medical examination, the synthesis of the report on forensic examinations carried out in Kosovo during 1999 of Dr. Baccard; the report of the MUP of Serbia about the examination of the scene in Kotlina in Kacanik, the 23rd of March, 1999; then a record compiled by Dr. Strbac and Dr. Tomasevic; and the statements of Thaqi Milazim, Draga Mustafa, and Hazbi Loku.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Waiting for the transcript -- okay, we have reached the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, those are all exhibits in these proceedings. The report for the Austrian team for Kotlina is P361; the report of the French team of Izbica is P209; the report of Dr. Baccard is P1809; the SUP Urosevac Kotlina forensic material is 6D 501; the videotape of Witness Liri Loshi is P232; the statement of Hazbi Loku, P2296; the statement of Mustafa Draga is P2244; the statement of Milazim Thaqi is P2246; and the pictures of -- that -- the previous statement of Milazim Thaqi is P227; and the Tomasevic-Strbac report of -- review of -- external review of corpses is P248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor Stankovic, if I could ask you some general matters first if we're going to the specifics of your findings or conclusions related to the matters in your report. Based upon your knowledge, experience, and expertise, is it possible within a degree of medical certainty accepted in the forensic science field of practice to ascertain a precise cause of death and circumstances where only skeletal remains are discovered where human tissue is sparse or gone, particularly differentiating between post mortem and antemortem damage and gun-shot as opposed to other injuries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say -- well, I will try in -- not to use any long words in my presentation in light of the report submitted by my colleagues and on the basis of what they described in the course of their processing of the remains and dead bodies at the sites where those bodies were found. At the same time, I have to say that the manner in which conclusions are formed, and I will say something more specific about that. Let me put it this way. It's not arbitrary, but at the same time if you bear in mind that all those autopsies were performed on the orders or at the request of such a high international body or institution such as the International Criminal Tribunal, if the injuries -- or rather, if those bodies were processed at the time when there were no combat activities going on and when there was enough time to record all the data important for determining the truth about the fate of those victims and to ascertain -- to ascribe the responsibility for those crimes, I think that this should have been done in a much more thorough manner than it -- than I was able to ascertain on the basis of my analysis. When we're talking about isolated cases of injuries, or rather, injuries on the bodies that do not have any soft tissue when there are no clothes, it is very difficult to draw any conclusions about those injuries except when we're dealing with injuries that leave visible traces on bones. And it is particularly difficult to draw conclusions about the causes of death, and it is also impossible to draw any conclusions on the basis of only those data on the relative positions of the assailant and the victim, and it is impossible to make any conclusions, for instance, on the basis of the putrefaction of soft tissues, about the calibre of the weapon with which those injuries were inflicted. I can speak about that in greater detail later, but this is what I can tell you in answer to your question at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What are the general or major concerns that you have about the methodology of work utilised by the forensic science professionals whose work you reviewed for purposes of preparing your analysis and expert report in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I will be very brief, but I have to note some specific examples of findings that were made both by the Swiss pathologists as part of the report submitted by the Austrian Ministry of the Interior and the conclusions by Lecomte and the way in which this was done by Baccard. For instance, at page 12 and 13 in the Serbian version, when describing the injuries or describing the remains we're talking about the dead body number 4 - that's Xhemajl Kuqi - one, and the same expert at page 1 in the first paragraph states the following: "On the torso, on the back to the right of the vertebral column, there was an injury visible, probably inflicted by a fire-arm." Mr. Markwalder then goes on, again in the part where he talks about the autopsy, says the following: "There were remains of explosives visible on the body. The lesions probably inflicted by shrapnel could be seen on the back." So one and the same doctor examining the body says in the first paragraph that this was a gun-shot wound, and in the last paragraph describing the autopsy, he says that the injuries were inflicted by mines or explosives. So to say the least, this is an error and an inconsistency that should disqualify him as an expert. What is even worse than that, the whole record of the autopsy has only two and a half sentences or two sentences. He says: "The body was whole all the way up to the head area. There were marks of explosives on the body," and the sentence that I just read out, "superficial lesions could be observed on the back, probably caused by shrapnel." So this is really unacceptable, that this person who was given the mandate to discover how this man got killed, to do this in such a perfunctory manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] -- This is P361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, which paragraph of the report is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is the first section of the report dealing with the forensic report of the Austrian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which paragraph deals with body number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could this be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. For the interpreters' benefit, there's been no reference made so far by counsel to the report. I'm seeking clarification. When they wish to use the report, it will be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where is it referred to, sorry, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Body 4 is not specifically referred to in the report. I believe now he's giving general concerns about the methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, is your report not meant to deal with specific examples of inadequate examination of bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if one examines a dead body, he's duty-bound, first of all, to provide the basic characteristics of the body being examined, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've misunderstood. I thought that you had provided us with a written report which reviewed the work of the Austrian Ministry of the Interior team investigating Kotlina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, all I'm asking is why is this particular example that you've been speaking about just now not dealt with in your report? I was looking -- that's what I've been -- I've been trying to find it, and I can't see it in the report. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, in that case, Mr. President, I would have to make an even larger report than the one done by the Austrian team about the examination of the bodies in Kotlina and to highlight all the inconsistencies contained in this report. In this specific case, I thought that I could present it in this manner. If necessary, I can deal with it at a later stage and then submit it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... general conditions with respect to P361, which is, in fact, the Austrian medical report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've obviously misunderstood what this document amounted to. That was all. I thought this was a thorough review of the work of the other team, and you're telling me these are only examples of your criticisms and that you have far more. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the course of my analysis of the reports that I listed at the beginning, I saw a number of inconsistencies and conclusions that were not in line with the usual forensic medical practice. On the basis of this, I was able to provide this report that is rather general, and it should be supplemented by the information that I am now providing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're saying in relation to this particular body there's no possibility that there were two separate causes of injury, a fire-arm or explosive device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am saying that one and the same expert, a doctor that performed the autopsy, in the first paragraph notes that this was an injury caused by a projectile; and at the end when he presents his autopsy report, he notes that the injury was caused by shrapnel. So for one and the same injury, he stipulates that this injury could have been caused by two different kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're satisfied he's talking about the same injury. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stankovic, is your criticism of the -- of this particular ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I think we should examine Markwalder's report on this very specific report you've mentioned, and let's see if it is -- let's see it on the screen and then read the results. But I feel, Professor, that while speaking of a projectile, I mean, a shrapnel is also a projectile, and a bullet can also be a projectile. There wouldn't be much of a difference, but a wound caused by either of these may differ because charring, because of the shape, because of the visible marking on the bone, and so on and so forth. But how he differed, we'd like to see it right away and examine this document. I think it'll be very important while you are present here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you identify the exhibit and the paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Again, this is P361, the Republic of Austria reports of crime scene team, and in English it's pages 12 to 13 just as in the B/C/S, item number 4, Kuqi Xhemajl. This takes the bulk of page 12 and goes on to the first half of page 13 before body number 5 is discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to answer this question posed by His Honour. First of all, in the first paragraph a mention is made of a fire-arm, not of artillery weapons. And fire-arms fire projectiles, whereas artillery weapons fire what we call mines and explosives. So in the first paragraph, he talks about fire-arm, and in the last one he talks about the explosives. So there are similarities and differences between those kinds of injuries, but this is at any rate a serious departure from the usual way in which injuries are described and classified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your understanding that Dr. Markwalder was present when the body was exhumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at any rate, he had to have been there if he was able to describe those injuries to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but in the report it looks as though the conclusion about a bullet wound which was a presumption may have been made by someone unprofessional in the forensic medicine sense exhuming the body and that the position was clarified by the autopsy. Is that the wrong way to read the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a person signs a report where he actually co-signs it, he is duty-bound to perform a full examination of everything that is written in the report and then to correct it as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think the only -- Professor, were you kindly speaking of body 4, were you, while presenting a critique of -- is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand. Now, here it says at the last paragraph before the description of the body is given: "A hole, presumably a bullet wound, was visible in the torso on the back to the right of the spinal column." Now, who could have written these remarks? You think this was Dr. Markwalder or just somebody who saw the body and passed it on later for the test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say because I didn't perform this kind of analysis, nor was this part of my task. I'm only speaking about what is stated when the injuries found on the corpse -- on corpse number 4 are described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And then we go to the autopsy, the report reproduced by you, which says: "The body was practically complete as for the region of the head. Marks of an explosion and fire were present on the corpse. Superficial skin lesions were visible on the back, possibly splinter wounds." So how do you differentiate between these two? A whole -- you mean to say that he missed the factum of the hole which was stated in the first part which I read over to you? You mean he didn't carry it on here? That is what you mean, Professor? I'm talking of a comparison between the first paragraph and this last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is the following: What is stated here, and I'll be very open about it, practically means nothing. This could have been done by a layman who has completed eight years of primary education, and it's impermissible to treat a victim in this way and the last moment of that victim's life. It's impermissible to decide on the basis of this kind of description of injuries on the sentence to be awarded certain people. It's impermissible for a high-level professional body to allow experts to do their work in this way, and any further comment I might make would be even worse. I apologise for using such hard words, but a person who conducted autopsies while I was being shelled, and my findings contain all possible details as one can see. Even under shelling, I was able to include all details in my report, and yet here they were working in peacetime conditions, and they failed to include such details, and that is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, what is absolutely visible here is that this aspect of the hole which is mentioned in the first paragraph doesn't find a mention at the concluding paragraph. Am I right in understanding this? So he has omitted something, is it? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right when you say this. There is a wound in the back, but it's not the same thing to say that this wound was caused by a fire-arm, by a projectile or bullet, because someone would have had to fire such a projectile from a fire-arm. This is not the same thing as saying that the wound was caused by shrapnel coming from a shell or explosive device fired and which then exploded. If someone has to clarify this, when a wound is caused by shrapnel, the shrapnel is in the area of the wound, and it would not have been difficult in the case of this corpse to take a scalpel, make a cut, and see whether in the area of the wound there was a bullet or a piece of shrapnel, and then it could have been easy to state with precision the weapon that caused the injury. The person who did this, in this particular case Dr. Markwalder, is disqualifying himself in the case of every finding he made. I don't want to go into details and analyse each and every case, each and every corpse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm not understanding, I'm afraid, Professor, is why you say no victim should be treated in this way. What is it you say is the way in which the pathologist treated the victim in which is inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Mr. President, in the course of a conversation with a previous prosecutor of this Tribunal, Mr. Goldstone, I said in the course of lunch that I talked to my corpses, and he choked when he heard this. He thought that I was -- well, I won't say what he thought, but I explained to him that when you are conducting an autopsy, the victim is telling you about the last moments of his life. If you do not know how to register what the injuries rely, how they were inflicted, the manner in which they were inflicted, the mutual positions of the attacker and the victim, whether the victim suffered or not when the injuries were inflicted, whether death was instantaneous or whether it was protracted, you as Judges know that all these circumstances have an influence on sentencing. In a case like this, no one has the right and nowhere in the textbooks does it say that someone can describe a body as Mr. Markwalder says that it is entire up to the head. What about the head? What is this about? How can he describe this in just two and a half lines? This is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my main objection, and in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, the head was missing. He can't do anything about the head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that he should describe the head or bring it back; he should say that the mortal remains were of such and such a length, of such and such a mass. There is a protocol as to how mortal remains should be described in such cases. I don't even know, in spite of all my experience, and I've done over 5 or 6.000 autopsies. I don't understand what this colleague of mine was trying to say in these two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what he seems to have said is that there were signs of superficial injury on the body. I mean, what more is he saying than that? He's not saying the body was shot. All he's seen is marks on the corpse and superficial skin lesions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why didn't he examine the body in full? That's what he should have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to decide whether he was being realistic or not and acting properly or not when we hear all the evidence. There are some things, you know, in life that you have to take decisions about how you deal with, and perhaps he made a decision. We'll need to review that in the light of all that you say and all that he and others have said. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the record does report that the OTP's investigator was the one making the decisions for this investigation and all the exhumations at several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for all we know, budgets were involved. I don't know, but to -- I'm concerned that a professional would dismiss all the work of another person on the basis of a finding he made on one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the comments of the Professor are related to this particular report and the findings in this report that are being presented as positive evidence in this case, Your Honour. He's attacking the methodology of reporting, and as we'll go through this for -- as you'll see, he talks about the methodology of exhumation, et cetera. As a forensic science professional, he's questioning the value of this report, which is of critical importance to these proceedings, I think, and it's highly relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The person -- yes, he says the person who did this, in this particular case Dr. Markwalder, is disqualifying himself in the case of every finding he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because he's the autopsy physician who does the findings in this report. Every forensic section of this report, I believe, says Christopher Markwalder in P361, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That -- I find it difficult. It's like saying if a mistake is made or a witness tells a lie on one thing, then we shouldn't believe him on anything. I mean, that doesn't seem to me to be a reasonable way of going about things. You look at each individual case on its own merits. However, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, just hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to bother you with this question, Professor. Now, we've examined this and your critique, as well, but the flaw is that you have missed this in your own report. It's because of too much of reports there, and you wanted to give a brief report from your side. Could you please refer us to any similar example which is embodied in your report to suggest a similar circumstance and a similar critique on Dr. Walder so that we know that you took that in your report and displayed it. Could you kindly give us one more example of such a situation, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I will give you two such examples. I will demonstrate how a finding can make a situation more complex. If we take body number 7, Rexha Neshat, Mr. Markwalder says in his description or autopsy finding the following: "Traces of explosive fire were found on the body. The skull was broken by a blow from a blunt object. Due to the advanced putrefaction, it was not possible to establish whether the wound was inflicted during the victim's life or after his death" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Which paragraph in your report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, paragraph 10 of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, paragraph 10 of my report, and the Serbian, it's page 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, paragraph number should be good enough. This is the one which begins: "The fractures of the skull sustained when the body fell 6 metres ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that refers to body 7, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- 23, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Footnote 23, Your Honour. It identifies the bodies that are being analysed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the conclusion, it says that the skull was fractured by a blow from a blunt object, which means that somebody else inflicted the injury by using a blunt, hard object such as a rifle-butt or a plank, that somebody inflicted a blow on the victim on the head. And unfortunately, and this is part of my critique, we don't have a description of the appearance of the skull fracture. And such a skull fracture could have been caused, for example, if the victim had fallen 6 metres into the well when the body was thrown into the well. It could also have been inflicted by shrapnel, by an explosion. It could have been caused if the body was thrown to one side and hit something hard with the head. So there are several possibilities, several ways, in which this injury could have been caused. But here, only one possibility is given, indicating that somebody inflicted this serious injury on purpose, and this is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor. I just thought I should have it clarified. Now, obviously he was dead. Now, he died because of some cause, and that causes the broken skull. He was not coming alive for purposes of his medical examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just -- no. I think -- I'm afraid I disagree with my colleague because it's clear they acknowledge that the skull could have been fractured after death. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: How did he die then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what does it matter? He's not suggesting for one minute that there's positive evidence that this man was killed by a fracture of the skull. I think we should just proceed with the examination. We'll continue any further questions after the prosecution cross-examination if there's any other areas to be explored. It does at the moment, though, seem that very significant criticisms are being based on an interpretation of P361. That's not necessarily the interpretation that the Bench would place on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that the relevance of P361 that the Bench might have is not the same as the parties represent to it that as positive evidence might have of it, but we're trying to present a full overview of the various methodological and factual matters pertaining to the same that go towards what findings were either overlooked or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a great pity if such a dramatic criticism as the one made in relation to body number 4 is not in the report. The whole point about an expert report is to give full details to the Bench and the other parties of the really significant things that an expert witness is going to say, and that's as significant as anything else in that report. In fact, it might be more significant than most of the stuff that's in it. And it's difficult -- still difficult to understand why that wasn't dealt with in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stankovic, we've been dealing with for the most part paragraph 1 of your report where you talk about the various methodological differences -- deficiencies, I should say, of the Austrian team's report with respect to Kotlina. Let me ask you a follow-up question. Could you please tell us whether in your opinion the reasonable and commonly accepted standards of the forensic medical community were complied with in the processing of the corpses from Kotlina by the Austrian and the Swiss team as recorded in P361?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that standards were not observed. My objections consist of the following: It is impermissible to take that attitude when examining mortal remains during autopsy. I saw this several times, that the post mortem record consists of two and a half lines or a maximum of four lines describing the injuries and explaining the cause of death of certain individuals. That is why I placed this objection. If necessary, I am prepared to interrupt this testimony of mine and in a short period of time, say a month, I can provide you with all the inconsistencies contained not only by these findings but the other ones that I dealt with. I'm afraid that this way we are going to spend a long period of time dealing with this, and these are very clear things. I will be examined on things that are very clear. I don't think that in any country there can be such sparse descriptions provided by the autopsy experts involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can move on, I'd like to move on to paragraph 2 of your report, the next in the sequence --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I have an objection to the findings and conclusions in relation to Izbica as well as Mr. Baccard's conclusions. Should I present that now or at some other moment? I think that these objections are also fully justified and very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I would save those for later for the sake of trying to get through as much as this material as possible, since we do have, as you know, Doctor, lots of other very important points that I know you want to make about this other material. So right now, I would like to stay with Klina for the moment, and with regards to item 2 of your analysis or report, what is the -- do you have anything to add, and what is the precise nature of the parallel point that you're drawing based upon the material that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, as I looked at the material that had been provided to me, I noticed that the Urosevac MUP, that is to say the Ministry of the Interior in Urosevac, on the 24th of March, 2008, carried out an examination of the terrain where the corpses had been found around the well in the village of Kotlina. And on the basis of that, on the basis of these photographs that were made on that occasion, I tried to see whether any of the described corpses, or rather, the described clothes on the bodies that were examined and that were taken out of the wells correspond to the description of the clothes that can be seen on the photographs of the members of the Urosevac MUP taken when examining this locality. I established that there are reasonable grounds to believe that body number 7 that can be seen in the trench close to one of the wells is actually the body whose clothing was described in L7, so that is Rexha Neshat's body. I allowed for the possibility that during the time of inspection, this well was whole, the bodies hadn't been thrown into it, and that can be seen on the basis of the documentation collected at the time. And that is the conclusion I reached on the basis of the autopsy and the description of the clothing and what can be derived from the documentation of the MUP of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the transcript, at page 24, line 21, the witness was talking about the 24th of March, 1999; 2008 is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness himself said 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could move on to paragraph 3 of your report, I believe this is another observation about the items reported in P361, the Austrian report on Kotlina. Could you describe for us the significance of the fail -- or the lack of a finding of traces of projectile or fragments of mines or explosives on the vegetation surrounding the upper and lower wells?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When we were the -- when we were searching the terrain looking for mass graves, we did that together with members of the Ministry of the Interior or people who are involved in investigations and inquiries. In all these cases when we could not locate the graves, on the basis of the damage sustained by trees, vegetation, the bark on the trees, we registered the places that were execution sites or where these persons had lost their lives. In this specific case, bearing in mind that it is claimed that these persons were found in a well and executed in the vicinity of a well, the photo documentation of the MUP of Urosevac and the examination that was carried out by the Austrian investigators do not show any damage whatsoever on the vegetation there, or rather, it wasn't described; and if it wasn't described, it doesn't exist. There is no damage described sustained from projectiles or shells and explosives and explosive devices on the vegetation there, the trees, in the surroundings of the well, which indicates either that there was no execution on that site or these investigators did not register that. However, this is not contained in the report of the Austrian investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just take you back briefly to what you said about the Ministry of the Interior report. That's the Urosevac MUP report. They examined the terrain, and you've seen photographs of corpses in their report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was done to carry out post mortem examinations at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you that. I just looked at the material that was provided to me by the Prosecution and that was submitted to me for my examination. I cannot say what happened after that. I'm just speaking on the basis of the material I have and the material that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, staying with this finding at item 3, Professor, based upon your knowledge, experience, and expertise in the forensic community, is the finding or the lack of a finding of traces of projectile or fragments of mines or explosives in the vegetation indicative of a primary or a secondary grave-site?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: A lack of damage on trees and vegetation indicates that persons probably did not die at that location but elsewhere, that there was no execution there at that particular place, and that some of the bodies that were found there were most probably victims of armed struggle or something like that, that they were brought from somewhere else, especially those that had serious destruction sustained, like missing lower limbs, which indicates that that is an effect of shells and explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are these two separate possibilities that are being presented, that they were killed elsewhere and brought to that scene or that they died in an armed conflict? Are these two separate possibilities that you're posing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two separate possibilities. The photographs of the Urosevac MUP show I think three bodies that are in the area surrounding the grave-site, and most probably these bodies died there within armed struggle or in some other way. I cannot say that. However, what is evident is the lack of a large number of bodies on that location, especially bodies on which wounds derived from shells and explosives were registered. So the 20 or so bodies that were described in the autopsy report, that's what I mean. Some were brought from elsewhere, some of the bodies, and buried there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, in item 4 you give a very concrete analysis of the manner in which the Austrian report records the findings of soot-covered clothing fragments. I would like to ask you as a follow-up, what about biological and other traces? Did the site of the well exhibit any of these types of traces according to the reports reviewed by you, and what does that tell you according to your expertise and the commonly accepted principles of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area around these wells, there were no biological traces registered like blood, body parts, other biological traces that I could speak of. They were not found, they were not described, and they constitute a major problem in terms of where it was that death had occurred. The bodies found in the well, where did these people actually die? On the basis of this, it seems that death happened elsewhere, not in these wells. The traces of clothing that were registered, but it was not noted how far away they were from the well. These carbonised or charred remains were found in the well itself. Does that mean on the basis of what is described here that the bodies were brought in from some other territory and thrown into the well? This is supported by the fact that there are traces of charred or carbonised parts of clothing that were found in the well. There are statements to the effect that they were thrown in the well and that explosive devices were thrown in, too, that caused these injuries that were described on the bodies from the well. However, bearing in mind the location where these parts of clothing were found, they could not have gotten out from deep down, 6 metres down, where the bodies were found as described in the investigator's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And a follow-up question for that, Professor. Had the victims, had they met their end in the well, their -- had the fatalities occurred in the well according to explosives where there are missing body parts, would there still be some biological traces of those body parts within the well that would have been discovered by a properly -- by a forensic review of the site? That is to say, is it possible for all biological evidence of a head to disappear in an enclosed area such as a well subject to an explosion without leaving any biological traces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the depth at which the first mortal remains were found of the bodies that were found in the well, it is impossible to expect, in view of the breadth of the well, that they could have been ejected out of the well to other areas outside of the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at item 5 of your report, could you please explain for us what you specifically mean when you say that an inexpert method of exhuming the bodies indisputedly led to destruction of many important traces of evidence in the Kotlina investigation. What precise procedural deficiencies were there in this regard, and what are the consequences upon -- of the same in your opinion upon the reliability of the findings contained in this investigative report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When work started in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we started doing those autopsies, but when first the commission was established followed by this Tribunal, then the methodology was prescribed, how to process mass graves. The methodology that was accepted by Professor Wright, Australian Professor Wright, set out the acceptable manner in which mass graves need to be processed and the way in which this archaeological work has to be done. At that time, the teams from The Hague Tribunal were already doing field work, processing a large number of mass graves, and it is not clear to me how this methodology for processing mass graves could be departed from. And the most unorthodox error was to use the manual workers who actually do -- who actually dig out the graves can do that not in the presence of an expert. How can these people know what bullets look like, what projectiles are, whether we're dealing with body parts of humans or animals? And now the investigators themselves at pages 7, 17, and 70 describe that when they reached the area, the wells had already been exhumed up to the depth of 6 metres and that the workers continued doing the exhumations in the absence of expert personnel even when they were already there. So I can make this objection to the way in which this mass grave was exhumed, but as a lay person, not as an expert, I find it hard to accept a fact. In the soil that was dug out of the one of the wells, a bullet was found, and it was analysed in the forensic or ballistic laboratory in Austria, and it turned out that this bullet was made in China, made in 1964. That's at page 4 of the report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 104 of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very important when we're describing the manner in which these people were killed, were these people killed in the fighting because it is very well known that the FRY army and the Serbian Ministry of the Interior did not have this kind of ammunition. This ammunition was used by Albanians. Albania had this ammunition, and its use was recorded in Kosovo. So perhaps it was possible that in an exchange of fire or in cross-fire of sort, a person could have been hit by mistake and then buried in the well. So this is the basic remark one has to make, to say that the procedure that is stipulated by the Tribunal itself for the way in which mass graves are to be processed was not adhered to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please help us to be specific. When was that procedure stipulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this procedure was in place when in 2001 I appeared before this Tribunal. At that time, Mr. Wright was already working on mass graves in Srebrenica, and this is when this methodology was stipulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... investigation was in 1999, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the Kotlina investigation in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Kotlina investigation was carried out in 1999, but the mass graves around Srebrenica were done in other sites before 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was there a methodology established for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all of us who worked on those mass graves did it in accordance to our training. We all devised our own methodology, but at the point when the Tribunal in The Hague accepted this methodology such as processing mass graves and archaeological exhumations that were first proposed by Australian Professor Wright, we accepted that, and we applied the same methodology to any further work on mass graves. So it is quite incomprehensible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when did Professor Wright devise his methodology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was in 1996, 1997, something like that, but that was at any rate prior to this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that -- was that the recognised method that ought to have been used at that time by those exhuming bodies in connection with Tribunal investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at any rate it was an experienced expert who based on his authority, his knowledge, his previous work determined the way that all of us worked, and at the same time an institution such as the Tribunal in The Hague has to have if not identical then at least similar methodology in place for crime scene processing. I have to say that although I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just try to answer my questions, please. And where in your report do you deal with this failure to apply accepted, recognised methodology devised by Professor Wright?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not saying that the methodology devised by Professor Wright was not used because there are other methodologies, but in paragraph 5 of my opinion I state that unprofessional procedure was used in the exhumation of the bodies in Kotlina. I find it hard to believe that somebody may not notice or if somebody is working on the exhumation of bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please try to answer the questions I'm asking you. You've been giving us very, very long answers on matters when you've been asked fairly specific questions at times, and it doesn't help. You see, we've got this very long answer about methodology, and it's been necessary for me to ask a number of questions to try to find out where this standard is set down if there is such a standard and whether we should be recognising it and applying it to our own investigations here. Now, Mr. Ivetic, are you intending to go through this report paragraph by paragraph in the way that you've started?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not all but most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've only got a half an hour left, I think, on your estimated time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so you will have to devise a way of focusing the issue. The questions the Bench have asked in this case are as a result of the report not dealing with matters which are fundamental. So please -- you're obviously going to take longer than that. I -- it's easy to see that, but you have to focus the issues. The -- we know that there are hundreds of pages on this topic and that we could spend our lifetimes analysing forensic science investigations in the case alone, but we have to bring reality to bear. Professor, we have to have a break at this stage. It's routine. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break, and we'll resume again at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, my colleagues are pointing out a transcript situation. Page 30 of today's transcript, line 16, the doctor referenced page 7, 17, and 70, and the 7 and 17 were co-joined to make it 717. So the correct citation should be pages 7, page 17, and page 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hello again, Professor. If we can continue. Moving along to item 6 of your analysis of the Kotlina site. You give findings about the number of bullet cartridges that were found as opposed to the number of bullet wound entries recorded by the forensic professionals at the site. In your opinion, based upon this material evidence, is this indicative of an execution site or of some kind of secondary grave-site?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area around the well, 12 spent shell cases were found, and in the bodies of the persons who were killed and exhumed from the well, at least 26 gun-shot wounds were found, which indicates that the gun-shot wounds were inflicted somewhere else. And after that, the bodies were brought to the well and thrown in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, item 7 is a follow-up to that where you talk about the positioning of body parts and carbonised clothing. Could you tell us what these -- what these factual circumstances lead you to believe -- how they lead you to believe that the explosive entries occurred outside of the premises of the well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: If the parts of the body that have been destroyed are in the deepest layer and then in the central layer most preserved bodies are found and then bodies that -- body parts that were destroyed are again found on the surface level, that indicates that the explosive injuries were -- came into existence somewhere else. Otherwise, the worst injuries would be in the surface layer followed by those in the central layer and only then in the deepest layer. Those would be the least serious injuries, but in this case, this was not verified, which shows, which indicates that the bodies were brought from somewhere else and thrown into the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does the positioning of -- does the positioning of the small body parts lead you to any conclusion as to whether this is a primary or a secondary grave-site?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The position of the bodies that were found in the well and bodies 6, 12, and 13 in particular indicate that during the exhumation the corpses were leaning with the front part of the body against the ground. Explosive injuries were described in the front of the body. If the bodies had been in the well and then an explosive device thrown in, it would have been logical for the injuries to be in the back, not the front, of the bodies, bearing in mind the position in which the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have reviewed the statement of Hazbi Loku as to how he said these victims met their end. Does the forensic evidence as recorded in the reports of the team, the Austrian team, support Mr. Loku's account of how these persons met their end in the well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As for Loku's statement, what I can say is that much of it is untrue or does not correspond to what was registered by the forensics experts of the Austrian team or to what can be seen in the photographic documentation of the Urosevac MUP, nor does it correspond to the manner in which the persons found in the well were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And item 9 of your report appears to be referring again to your finding that the injuries could not have been inflicted by a bomb in the well. The question I have for you, sir, is relating again to the nature of the grave-site at item 11 of your report. You explain how you interpret the evidence of a hand being found at a depth of 8.2 metres in the well and leg and stump found at 9.3 metres of the well. In your opinion, does the investigative team undertake appropriate forensic analysis to consider or exclude the significance of these findings as to regards -- as regards to whether this is a site of execution, a primary or secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, if a body part such as a fist was found at 8.2 metres in depth and the other parts of the bodies such as the right leg and another part were found at 9.3 metres and between the body parts that were found there is 1.1-metre layer of soil, this shows that the mortal remains were buried in different time-periods as they were found in the locations where they were located previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the paragraph 13 where the medical examiners were unable to ascertain whether the injuries were inflicted by a fire-arm or as a result of the explosion, although they had a metal detector at their disposal, what is the -- strike that. Based upon your knowledge and experience, would it be able to use common forensic techniques to determine the existence of either shrapnel or projectiles, and to what do you attribute the reported failure to find those on such a closed -- enclosed location such as a well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: This remark is contained in the superficial processing of the mortal remains. If the person who conducted the autopsy of this body had made an incision with a scalpel in the area where wounds were registered in the front part of the stomach, if the wound had been caused by shrapnel, they would have found pieces of shrapnel there. If the wound had been caused by projectiles, they would have found the projectiles, or they could have established that there was an entry/exit wound. They could also have made X-rays because it's not the same whether an injury was caused by a fire-arm projectile or an explosive device or a shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your questions so far since the break have all simply resulted in repetition more or less of what's in the report. That's not an appropriate way to deal with this. It's striking that this is a witness who's being very critical of the brevity of the reports of others, and he himself has - for reasons which may not be entirely his fault - presented a report, which is fairly brief, it would appear, when it comes to looking more closely. But that's something you're going to have to live with and try to get through this now within a realistic time-scale. But the Chamber's not willing to listen to constant repetition of what's already in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet when we go to something outside the report, Your Honours, you want to know where it is in the report. I'm at a loss to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, indeed, because significant things are not dealt with -- this should all have been dealt with in the report in a way that would enable you to stand up, ask a few questions, sit down, allow cross-examination, and then re-examine on the things that have been focused as real issues in the cross-examination. But to go through a report like this chapter by -- paragraph by paragraph and get most of the -- and find that most of the evidence is repetition of what's in here is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I was guided by Your Honour's own comments with respect to what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you're in difficulty because of the inadequacy of the report, but please do your best to try and make the most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can then go to something that's not in the report, Professor. P361, page 17 in the B/C/S, pages 16 through 17 in the English. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Chapter numbers are good enough or paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, they're not. Right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- paragraphs, so I have to do it this way. It's the crime scene XX -- 21-1, upper well, 11th September 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see here, sir, that when the team arrived at the site, the builders reported that the workers exhumed further body parts, three hands, decayed flesh and bones. After the site team stopped work on 10 September 1999, these hands were no longer at the site, and their exact location could not be traced at the site. Do you have any opinion as to what this indicates of the method or matter in which the exhumations were performed at the site, Professor Dr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: 17, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Serbian it's page 17, and it's Prosecution Exhibit 361.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that my remarks concerned primarily the methods used here, the methodology used during the exhumation, and the autopsies, the examination of the bodies. The main summary of my report is to the effect that the victims were not executed near the well and that the explosive injuries were not created inside the well. To prove this, each of these paragraphs contains a fact in support of this view, and that is the purpot of my whole report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that you've been asked is whether the fact that body parts initially discovered were later no longer there and could not be traced indicates something about the method of exhumation. Now, could you deal with that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic will repeat his question, but you were answering something that wasn't asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please just repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As soon as I find my place in the transcript, I will repeat it. I want to make sure -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at page 17 in the Serbian of the Austrian report, it is indicated that when the team arrived at the site, the villagers reported that the workers exhumed further body parts, three hands, decayed flesh, and bones. After the site team stopped work on 10 September 1999, these hands were no longer at the site, and their exact location could not be traced at the site. What -- do you have any opinion as to what this specific fact indicates on whether -- on the question of whether the exhumations were performed in a manner that was in compliance with applicable forensic examination standards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that this does not comply with the standards of forensic medicine and the processing of a mass grave for exhumation of mortal remains to be done by labourers without the presence of experts such as investigators, forensic experts, doctors, and others who should be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can now turn to your examination of the reports relating to Izbica. I believe sections 1, 2, and 3 of your analysis in that regard are quite detailed and don't need to go -- don't need to be further developed here. Now, with regards to item 4 -- excuse me, with regard to -- first of all, with regard to the Izbica site, you earlier explained to us relative to Kotlina the significance of the number of recovered bullet casings and the number of entry wounds on the bodies. Do you have the same conclusion and analysis with regards to Izbica based upon the number of bullet wounds in the material and the number of recovered bullet -- recovered projectiles or bullet casings? Would the same forensic analysis apply?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, the same conclusion can be drawn. In the places marked as places where executions were carried out for persons from the village of Izbica, of those persons, 84 spent shell casings were found - one was from a sniper rifle - and the number of persons killed or buried was about 137, as mentioned in the report. Therefore, evidently there is a discrepancy between the number of spent shell casings and the number of persons who were killed and buried in the mass grave in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just finish up with the report before going on to other matters. In paragraphs 7 and 8 of your report relating to Izbica and your analysis of the forensic materials compared to the testimony of Mr. Thaqi, do you have any additional analyses to add to the discussion relating to Mr. Milazim Thaqi and his account of how events occurred based upon the forensic evidence available?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I deliberately mentioned these three statements that I dealt with. In addition to this, I have to say that it's not possible for the statements of Milazim Thaqi to be covered by the data done by Dr. Tomasevic and Dr. Strbac, the autopsy they did. This statement does not correspond with the statement. So when we are dealing with spent shell casings, if there had been a shower of bullets, if the machine-gun had fired constantly, if there had been too many projectiles, we can see whether this is true or not by the number of spent shell casings and the number of injuries on the bodies. And Thaqi's statement as to how he escaped and how he had damage on the -- on his pullover, well, if this had happened then his tissue would also have been injured. There would have been an entry wound, a gun-shot wound, and you cannot find any traces of blood on the pullover. So there's nothing to support his claim that the damage to the pullover was caused in the manner he described.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you spent a great deal of time analysing the video of Liri Loshi, identified as exhibit P232, purporting to show the discovery of bodies at three alleged killing sites, Izbica. You have selected and gone through with me the following video images from that exhibit, which I would now as for you to review, and then if you can explain for us what is the forensic significance of what we are seeing, the forensic medical significance of what we are seeing, and what opinions or conclusions you draw from the same, and if you need to stop or rewind the video, if you could please just make the instructions by speaking aloud, and I believe my colleague will be able to accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, this is Exhibit P232. In line with what we have done with previous witnesses, this is identifying the exact minute and second locations of that video, and this particular excerpt, which perhaps we might give a separate exhibit number, I don't know, it's up to Your Honours, are just the images -- for sake of time, not going through the whole video, but just the images that the doctor selected during proofing that he thought illustrated important points with respect to whether or not these are -- whether or not these are corpses in their original positions at original killing sites or something other. So at the conclusion, if you feel we need to introduce this as a separate exhibit, it can be done. It's a stand-alone video file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can begin, Doctor, with the first clip and if you can begin your commentary and discussion as to what is medically shown to us and what that can lead you to conclude based upon a reasonable degree of forensic medical certainty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see a group of corpses here in a wood surrounded by vegetation, and the appearance of the bodies in the lower part is characteristic. The last body down in the valley, you can see that it's lying on its back and that post mortem rigidity has set in, and this shows that the body was moved because of the poor quality. You cannot see any traces of blood or of spent shell casings, but because the legs are rigid and they are raised up into the air, as is the arm, this shows that the body was moved. It could not have been in this position after the inflicting of the wounds and after -- before rigidity set in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was the section at 1120.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. The second clip goes from 1333 to 1342, if we can play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, again, if you advise us what we are seeing from a medical standpoint and what that leads you to conclude based upon your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a technical question. Now, you talk of the body rigidity or rigor mortis, as we call it. Does it stay permanently? I don't think so. Will it stay permanently, the stiffness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Rigor mortis sets in first in the heart 30 seconds after death starts, and then two hours after death it starts, and it lasts up to four hours; the body is stiff. Now, the rigidity depends on whether the body is moved and what the weather conditions are like, but again, it depends on the temperature and -- the outside temperature. But after 24 hours or 38 hours, there is no more stiffness. The body is flaccid -- well, it is a dead body that is no longer rigid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, but then the posture we saw of the legs, how will that stay because ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is possible because the front part of the body was turned on the surface. It was lying on the surface, and after that the body was moved. The body was moved from a particular position or from a particular locality or perhaps from the same place where it was then. But that is why there is this kind of rigidity. What I'm saying is that the body had been moved after death had set in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do I gather that that might simply have been to turn the body over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could play the next clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a male corpse as well. On the front right-hand side of the face, we can see that there are dry leaves sticking to it, which means that the body had been moved from its original position and that beforehand the front right-hand side of the body had been lying on a surface. It can also be seen on the basis of rigor mortis and the way the -- in which the right hand looks as well as the lower right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to the third clip, 1836 to 1850.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, it's a male body, and in the right-hand half of the face we can see liver mortis. The body is again in a position that shows that it had been moved. Before this picture was taken, the front part of the body was lying on a surface. So this is liver mortis, what -- the stains on the face that can be seen. I can give an additional explanation. It was described as blows to the front right side of the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... two or three more clips.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, a body on which we see a glove. A stiff male body, and we see some damage on the clothing, probably due to a wound that was bleeding. And above the left hand we can see a glove, probably belonging to the person who had manipulated the body. Probably beforehand, the body was reclining on a surface on the front side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Doctor, thus far have we seen any evidence of biological remains, blood, et cetera, bullet casings, et cetera, around these corpses to indicate to you that this is the actual site where they met their end?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the photographs we've seen so far, we did not see any biological remains as far as I could notice in this short span of time, and we didn't see any casings or any other weapons that may have inflicted the wounds or implements that may have inflicted the wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the timing of that one, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I missed it. If we could move back, we could find it. Just a little bit more. 1953 -- there it is, Your Honour, 1953 to 20 minutes. I believe we have a fifth and a sixth clip, if we can perhaps play those side by side.
