I believe they're a continuation of the same location -- the location -- the fifth and sixth clip, I believe, are in the same grouping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- well, 812 and 813.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right, and then 813 to 824.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What do we see here, doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could play it through to the end, I think that would be the end of this clip, and that's --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: What we see here -- well, underneath these bodies that can be seen on the video footage, what is noticeable are the blankets on which the bodies had been carried. So this can be evidence that the bodies were brought from a different area and placed here where the pictures were taken. You can see here by the body itself, you can see a blanket. Again, there are no biological remains there; there is no blood on the ground; there are no casings or anything else that would indicate what it was that inflicted the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does the state of the bodies in rigor mortis coincide with their physical location as depicted in the video -- that is to say, is their actual depth position accurately shown by the video based upon the evidence of rigor mortis and positioning of this body on the left? If we can go back, the legs --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that in this particular case rigor mortis shows that the body was lying on a surface, the front part of the body was, and it means that the body had been moved from a different location or from this area where the picture had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you very much, Doctor, and I know you looked at a lot -- the entire video multiple times to find the easiest way to highlight your points, and I thank you for taking that effort with me to shorten the time that we have to spend -- of the Trial Chamber's time that we have to spend. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to have that presented as a separate exhibit, which you can upload later today, or it's already uploaded, so we just need to give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe so. As soon as my colleague gets back, maybe we can get the next 6D number for that -- or we'll advise the Court of the 6D number for that and make a filing just to identify that for the record so it gets properly tracked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. A filing's unnecessary if you just tell us at an appropriate stage in the proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I get that information while I'm on my feet, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or even tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's 6D 1663, Your Honours, is the next available 6D number, and that will be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It will have that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor Dr. Stankovic, earlier today you indicated today that you still had some criticisms or objections about some of the other forensic work done in the Prosecution exhibits, and I told you we wanted to get through some of the material as much as possible. Now, I ask you if you could, please, briefly highlight for us your concerns, the basis for the concerns, and what they mean to you from a medical forensic standpoint.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: My basic premise and the fundamental conclusion I drew here is primarily that the mass grave in the village of Kotlina was not processed in the right way. A series of omissions were registered that I referred to in my report. During the post mortem, the description goes against all the generally accepted methods of carrying out post mortems and describing wounds on dead bodies. It is a fact that the conclusion that there had been an execution is based on non-material evidence; rather, the statements of certain witnesses who say inter alia, as in the case of corpse 24, that they saw when a bullet was fired into his head, and the post mortem establishes that there is only one wound in the left-hand side of the chest at that, so somebody is not telling the truth. Is it the people who were working on this locality, on processing this locality, or is it the witnesses? That is something that should be assessed on the basis of all the information that exists in the case file. It would be best if the colleagues who worked on this and those who are challenging their findings would establish direct contact at a venue like this one and resolve all dilemmas. As for the locality of Izbica, again, there is material evidence that was presented, and there were conclusions that can be seen in the material of the OTP, and that is unacceptable. For example, the conclusion of the French investigating team describing the mortal remains of 28 persons. And in the conclusion -- or rather, they draw the conclusion that in the grave there were 137 bodies, I think, out of which 135 men and two women. On the basis of what material evidence, or are these conclusions based on what somebody said or what the person actually found? Secondly, there is something that cannot be understood, namely, that in these findings what is described in the report of the French experts that on the basis of the changes on the decaying wounds, the projectile calibre is established. I have never come across anything like that, but if a body is decaying and there is a wound on that body and the putrefaction leads to changes in the wound itself, so how can you establish on the basis of that what the calibre of the projectile was? And thirdly, if on the basis of video-clip somebody provides exclusive descriptions or descriptions of causes of death and assesses, like Dr. Baccard, on the basis of reports or on the basis of this footage that is of a low quality - I'm not denying its authenticity, though - and if on the basis of that they conclude that a person was mentally retarded, and we know what kind of forms and shapes a face can assume once rigor mortis sets in, we really wonder whether this can be taken as evidence or not. So this leads to the question of the responsibility of the person who wrote this, the person who assesses this, and the person who accepts this. In this specific case, I cannot accept that, and that is why I presented my own position before this Trial Chamber, and I am prepared to defend that position in all discussions with any experts anywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor and Doctor, not only for your time today, but I know the extensive time that you've spent with myself and others preparing for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would tender the report 6D 670 of Dr. Zoran Stankovic and would pass the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Professor, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a question, Professor. Now, one of the flaws -- one of the flaws you have pointed out in the report is that the eye-witness account differed with the autopsy. Now, that's no fault of the author of the autopsy because autopsy will be believed more than the witness if there is a dichotomy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, you're quite right because if Witness Hazbi Loku says that the person on page 40 - that was corpse 24, in Serbian - if he says that this person was hit by a bullet in the area of the head, and if the person conducting the post mortem does not establish that, then that proves that this witness should be ruled out and that his evidence should not be taken into account. I am not going to interfere. It is for you to decide whether you are going to reject witness testimony or the report of the expert, but it's obvious that somebody is not telling the truth. If somebody fires a bullet into somebody's head, that is a terrible crime; and if there is no such thing, I don't see why somebody would make a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you think, Professor, because of your expert knowledge, these reports ought to have also mentioned about whether the corpses were undergoing putrification and whether they had the colouration like blue and all staining on the body, and therefore would have -- should have determined the timings of the death possible, timings of the death? Do you think that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, among other omissions is the thing that you noted. At the same time, witness statements indicate that these people had been mistreated, hit with planks, that they were -- had been beaten by those people who later executed them; yet, in descriptions you don't have a single injury that would correspond with that. There are no haematomas described. Quite the opposite. Lividity is mistaken for haematomas. Had the person carrying out the autopsy made a cut in this tissue, that person would have been able to ascertain whether this was simple liver mortis or a haematoma caused by injury with a blunt instrument, and I am simply noting those omissions and the difficult situation that you're in where you have to draw your conclusions on the basis of this defective procedure, and I don't want to interfere with your conclusion-making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. I just want to follow-up on the last answer you gave while it's still on my screen. You talked about witness statements indicating that some of these people had been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis, could you just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, I was asking you about your last answer. You mentioned that regarding the Kotlina well bodies that witness statements indicated that some of these people had been mistreated, hit with planks, and beaten before they were executed. And you say: "Yet in descriptions you don't have a single injury that would correspond with that." Now, I thought you told us on body number 7 you have a skull fracture or a skull injury that appears to have been done with a blunt instrument. Wouldn't that be consistent with beating someone with a plank and hitting them on the head?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in his statement, Hazbi Loku - that's at page 6 in the Serbian language - says when they reached the edge of the pit the Serbs started pulling apart a wooden fence around it. That fence was made of wooden planks that were nailed together. If I look at that, if we look for that at the footage made by the Urosevac MUP, you cannot see any planks, any slats or anything. There are just branches --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, no, stop there. That's not my question. My question is: That skull injury identified by Dr. Markwalder, you said that there was no injury that could be consistent with beating with planks. Isn't that skull injury being described as having been caused by a blunt instrument, something that could have been caused by beating with planks? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: But there were no planks there. That's what I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, Professor, let me -- you obviously do not understand our system, and I thought you would since you had been here before to assist. But under the system we operate, the counsel, whether for accused or for the Prosecution, are the ones who principally determine what questions will be asked. Now, that's rather different from the system with which you are no doubt more familiar in domestic proceedings in your own country. The question you've been asked is a very specific question, whether that injury is consistent with being hit with a plank. You're not being asked whether there's evidence of planks around or not, and we're capable of assessing that aspect of the evidence when we come to look at the whole picture. But your job here today is to answer the specific questions that you are given, and I will be grateful to you if you will continue to do that, please. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell me if the injury described --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't see your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you to explain to me when I'm supposed to talk about general things and when I'm supposed to talk about specific things. In general terms this injury could [Realtime transcript read in error "would"] have been caused by somebody striking this person with a plank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could intervene for the translation. He said [B/C/S spoken] could, not would.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did say could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's all I'm asking, if it could. So, Doctor, there is at least one example of an injury that would correspond with that eye-witness report, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because the eye-witness said that the injury had been caused with planks that were removed from an area around the well. These are branches or sticks, as we call them, from the low vegetation around it, not planks. Planks could have been present at some other area but not at the well as could be ascertained on the basis of the footage made by the Urosevac MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What footage are you talking about, the nine or 12 photographs that are attached to that report in Exhibit 6D 501?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the photo file that I was given for my use that was made by the Urosevac MUP on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could that skull injury have been caused by one of the branches or sticks, as you referred to them, in the low vegetation around the well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the beginning of your testimony today Mr. Ivetic had you go through all the materials you reviewed in preparing your report. I take it that you weren't provided or you didn't see any videotapes or transcripts of the testimonies of Dr. Baccard, Dr. Tomasevic, or Liri Loshi from this case or the Milosevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the same, I think, you saw witness statements of Liri -- of Hazbi Loku and I think Milazim Thaqi, but you did not have a chance to review their testimonies in this trial or the Milosevic trial, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the autopsy findings in the Austrian forensic report concerning body 4, you mentioned that there seemed to be a problem in that there's an initial description of what someone describes as a possible bullet-hole. Let me find my English translation to make sure I'm stating it accurately because I'm worried --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 12, counsel, if it helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what page it is for you, Doctor. It's probably 12 or 13. Body number 4, Xhemajl Kuqi. "A hole, presumably a bullet wound, was visible in the torso on the right -- or on the back to the right of the spinal column." And then on the next page in English, page 13, under the autopsy remarks, Dr. Markwalder doesn't make reference to a bullet-hole, but he talks about "marks of an explosion and fire were present on the corpse with superficial skin lesions were visible on the back, possibly splinter wounds." I note, Doctor, on page 5 of this report in the English, there's a description of it. Report on the crime scene. I don't know if you can find that page. It says: "Evidence is recovered by the crime scene group Austria 2/1999," and it names five individuals. Do you find that page? I think that's it that you have now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: 7, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you could go back two pages. I think you have this page. There were -- yeah, on that page do you see in the left column the third block up: "Evidence recovered by," and it names five individuals, and then right below that it says: "Autopsies conducted by," and it names Dr. Markwalder and Dr. Wyler, right? The page you have on top now looks like the one I'm looking at in English. Is that what it says? Yeah. Did I state that correctly? Five persons are listed as being the ones, evidence recovered by, and then Dr. Markwalder and Dr. Wyler are the ones who conducted the autopsies, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And immediately below that, we see the time-period: The collection of evidence at the crime scene occurred between -- well, the 7th of September and the 9th and 15th of September, and autopsies were done at Kacanik cemetery between the 13th and the 16th. From that, it seems like it might be a reasonable conclusion that that description we have of the bullet-hole for body number 4 is a description that was probably done by someone gathering the evidence at the site where the bodies were as opposed to the autopsy remarks by Dr. Markwalder at the Kacanik cemetery. Would you agree with me that that's reasonable?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the question. Prosecution ought to know. It's their exhibit. They should be able to present us with that information without having us to guess. As Your Honour may recall, we objected to some of these exhibits based upon the fact that some of the evidence appeared to be -- some of the material appeared to be hearsay collected from other persons as opposed to professional opinions by the people involved. If we're going to revisit that issue, I mean, I think the Prosecution is not asking us to hypothesise as to what exactly this exhibit means, and it's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I move to strike that last comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection is repelled. This witness has proceeded on a basis -- on the basis of a conclusion he himself has appeared to made that both these statements are the responsibility of the one person, and the Prosecution are plainly entitled to challenge his understanding of the situation by relevant questions. The question that's been asked is in our opinion relevant and may be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, do you need me to repeat my question, or do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the question that you asked me. I did my analysis on the basis of the materials that I had here in front of me. This possibility that you put to me is possible, but it is unacceptable to put side by side such two assessments in such a report. When the person -- the person that described the injury on removing the body from the well should have indicated that there is an injury to the right side of the spinal column, and persons that will carry out the autopsy would describe this injury in detail. They will make the final determination as to the nature of this injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a question about your report, Exhibit 6D 670. Judge Bonomy made a comment that he thought that your report was a thorough review of the work of the other team, and you seem to be telling us that these were the only examples of your criticisms. But you said you had a lot more criticisms than what were in your report. My question is: What was your criteria for selecting those items that you put in your report? Did you pick the worst examples you found, or did you just take a random sample? What was your methodology in choosing examples for your report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in the course of my analysis of these cases, I applied the methodology that is applied in my country, and as a rule it is applied, in fact, throughout the world. I applied the methodology that the investigators from the Tribunal applied. I mentioned the methodology used by Hagland and Wright and other people who did those analyses and processed mass graves in the former Yugoslavia. At the same time, in this specific case I presented a striking finding and an omission that is inadmissible when a doctor is performing an autopsy. Perhaps I was too harsh in my words, but knowing this institution and having high regard for this institution, this Tribunal, and also for the persons who were involved in this autopsy and the victims, I wanted to use this example to show the contradictions inherent in one such report and to say that this is really incomprehensible. Because I hold you, Prosecutors, and the Trial Chamber in high regard, but I don't know in which country it would be possible to pass a judgement on the basis of such scant information and such perfunctory word and inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can intervene. I don't know. I haven't thought about whether this translation fits, as well, but at line 59, 10, the witness said [B/C/S spoken] in Serbian if it's presented as striking. Perhaps I can have the assistance of the translators what [B/C/S spoken] is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when you referred there to this specific case and presenting a finding and an omission that is inadmissible, were you talking about body number 4? Because you didn't appear to be answering the question that Mr. Hannis asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about body number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but the question Mr. Hannis was asking you was what criterion led to you including certain examples in your report but not including others, including body 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I picked a typical example that would be typical of the kind of examples that can be found in those cases. So after a full analysis, I presented a typical example of inconsistencies in an autopsy report if that is how one can put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still don't understand what you're saying I'm afraid. The striking -- well, the -- if it's typical rather than striking. The typical example of body 4, if it is the best example, why is it not in your report, and what is the criterion you were applying that led you to choose some examples in the report and not to refer to others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't provide all the examples in light of the limitations that were set to me in -- for the presentation in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were these limitations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was told that I was going to too great lengths, that I was providing examples that you couldn't look at, and that I would have one hour and a half for my examination, and I wanted to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand any of that. To enable you to be as brief as possible in court, then you should provide as full as possible a written report. We've got expert reports in this case that extend to over a hundred pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to write up a report of a hundred pages, but I was told it was not necessary, which is why I didn't include all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, in noting these shortcomings in the Austrian forensic report, did you personally make any effort to try to contact Dr. Markwalder to ask him about his findings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, for the simple reason that I felt that after my remarks he would respond to everything I said and that we could discuss all my objections and his findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't that have been helpful to you in understanding his report, to have a conversation with him, before finalising your report? He might have been able to clarify some of the things that were ambiguous to you in his report, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is clear to you from this autopsy finding. I apologise for having to be -- to speak in such terms, but nothing is clear to me from this. If someone can conclude on the basis of one and a half lines of an autopsy report on the causes of death, the injuries on the body, the weapons used to cause the injuries, the cause-and-effect relationship between the injuries and the death, the mutual positions of the attacker and the victim, and other things - I won't list them all so as not to waste your time - I don't know what I can discuss with someone concerning all of this. I don't know what there is here that is clear to everybody but me. I would like to have it put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, let me ask you. You say nothing was clear to you from this report. You would agree with me that regarding some of the bodies there was literally very little to work with, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For example, body number 8, page 18 going on to page 19 of the English, the autopsy, Dr. Markwalder notes: "Explosion and fire marks were found on the body. Most of the body was missing. Only remains of the legs, both feet, and various remnants of clothing can be accounted for. No bullet entry wounds were found." What more would you want or expect him to say in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take it in turn. First of all, on what parts of the body traces of explosives and gun-fire were found. If this is on the whole body --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Given the fact that the only remains are legs and both feet, I assume that explosion and fire marks were found on the legs and/or the feet, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these -- right now he's asking the doctor to say whether his assumption -- whether Mr. Hannis has made an assumption or not. That question is not proper. The doctor was appropriately answering the prior question, and I think Mr. Hannis's intervention is uncalled for. Let the doctor finish his analysis of what the question was, not asking him, Am I assuming this, Doctor? It's not a proper question for cross-examination, Your Honours, I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's impossible to tell at the moment whether the witness was, in fact, going to answer your question, Mr. Hannis; and therefore, he should be allowed to continue with his answer. So please continue, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the description when the remains of the legs, both soles of both feet and various pieces of clothing, it's necessary to describe what was left. Feet, are there injuries on the feet or not? Based on the disposition and localisation of injuries on the other parts of the body, one can say with a great degree of certainty what sort of explosive device was used, whether these were shells or bombs or dynamite or other explosive material, what pieces of clothing were found, what they looked like. We describe all of that, and we register all of that in our autopsy findings. I don't know about others, but I know that this is something that is prescribed in all of our rules. This is something that has to be done. I've looked at other autopsy reports that have to do with The Hague Tribunal, and I saw that all this is described in a great many of them by the forensics who did the report. So why was it not done in this case? That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, have you ever been a member of an international forensic medicine team conducting autopsies abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I can tell you that when I did autopsies in Vukovar where I was the chief of the forensics team, my work was evaluated by a UN team headed by Antonio Pegail [phoen], and they evaluated my work very highly, and it was done under extremely difficult circumstances while fighting was still going on. There was no electricity, no water. The temperature was below 20 degrees centigrade. After that and after all these examinations of mass graves, they were all attended by representatives of the international community, but the war that was going on in the territory of the former Yugoslavia made it impossible for me to be part of an international forensic team conducting such work on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And the joint activities in dealing with mass graves and corpses on the territory of my former state is something I was not in -- did not have the opportunity to participate in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Professor, there is no need to expand in that way, and indeed, it's very easy to understand that your work would be commended by others, but what we are trying to do is establish the correct approach to be taken to a situation. The situation you describe and your own work is some guide to us, but I was concerned to know whether you had been involved in any other similar operation elsewhere. We recognise the depth of your experience from the very fact, as I think you indicated at the beginning, you carried out more than 5.000 autopsies yourself. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, I apologise for jumping the gun when you were trying to answer my last question. In your report, Exhibit 6D 670, paragraph number 10 on the Kotlina report, you talk about: "The fractures of the skull sustained when the body fell 6 metres which occurred as the injured part of the head hit objects in the well such as stone could equally have been inflicted if the body smashed into hard body parts of bodies thrown in the well earlier, such as a knee, elbow, head, or similar." And then there's a footnote 23, which refers us to body number 7 on page 16 of the English, which is that injury we've talked about before, the skull was broken by the force of an adult blow. And it also refers us to body 17, page 30. Now, I'm looking at body number 17 on page 30, and that's referred to as the autopsy of Agim Loku. Dr. Markwalder did this one. He says: "There were marks of an explosion and fire on the body. Most of the body was missing. Only the remains of the head, throat, right shoulder, and upper right arm survived. There was a gun-shot wound on the upper right arm." I don't see any reference to a skull injury. Is that a mistake in your report? Is there a typo? Should it be a different body number, a different page number? What's happened there? I don't have the B/C/S in front of me. Maybe there's a translation error on body numbers or page numbers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Body number 16, that's body number 16. There's an error here, a typographical error. It says 17. That's a typographical error. It should say 16, where it says the skull was fractured due to a blow with a blunt object inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is this a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, we have to have another break at this stage for half an hour, so could you again please leave the court with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, in paragraph 2 of your expert report, 6D 670, you say: The clothes described on body number 7 -- in Exhibit P361, the Austrian forensic report, you say: The clothes described on that body number 7 and the head injury correspond to the body in photographs number 11 and 12 of the photographic documentation of the Urosevac SUP, which is Exhibit 6D 501. How can you tell us that the head injury described in the Austrian forensic report matches what you see in the photographs number 11 and 12 of the MUP Urosevac SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that this is a typographical error because I found the correspondence in clothing described in body number 7 compared to the documentation in the Urosevac SUP, and this is a typographical error, which I now wish to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the phrase "and the head injury" should not be in there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it shouldn't be in there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that's the second typographical error we've discovered in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were you able to determine that the clothing in those photographs from the Urosevac SUP report correspond to the description of the body number 7 in the Austrian forensic report? I mean, in the photograph you're only able to see basically the outer layers of clothing, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and based on the external appearance of the clothing, that is trousers made of blue cloth, a reddish item of clothing, reddish-brown, a reddish-brown denim jacket on the upper part of the body, this indicates that this might be body number 7. That's why I allowed for this possibility, that it was body number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I understand it, the Urosevac photos are from late March 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in doing -- are you familiar with the process, the procedures, of an on-site investigation like this by the Urosevac SUP? What would be done with the bodies after the evidence was gathered and the photographs were taken? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I conducted my expertise based on the materials in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't have any particular expertise in clothing, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I can register with my eyesight the colour of the clothing that the corpse had on because we describe this whenever we conduct an autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be unusual for MUP to leave the body there so that it's discovered in the well almost six months later when the Austrian forensic team is doing its exhumation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The answer at line 67, 20, said he has no knowledge of on-site investigations, so this question is without foundation and calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I would expect, given the work he's done and the positions he's held, he might be in a position to opine whether a body that's the subject of an on-site investigation is left where it's found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't you think it might be a better question to ask if he doesn't find it strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I could ask if it's standard procedure to leave bodies out at murder scenes after an investigation is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Standard procedure implies that the bodies in wartime conditions -- well, the clothing should be described, all the parameters that would later be needed for identification should be recorded, and then the bodies should be buried in the closest possible spot, and the spot should be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's really no way you can say to a reasonable certainty on medical or scientific grounds that the body you see in the photograph from the Urosevac SUP is the same body that's described as body number 7 in the Austrian forensic report, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that with a hundred per cent certainty, but only with a certain degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that the photo documentation of the Urosevac MUP doesn't show any damage to the vegetation around the well and that there was none described in the Austrian investigator's report. At page 26, line 10, you said: "And if it wasn't described, it doesn't exist." Isn't another possibility that there may have been some damage but it was not portrayed in the limited number of photographs that were taken by the Urosevac SUP? Isn't that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said in my first statement either it didn't exist or it was not recorded by those who conducted the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Another possibility is that the -- any explosions and damage to surrounding vegetation might have occurred after the photographs were taken and before mid-September when the exhumations took place, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. The doctor testified that the Austrians did not note any either, so is counsel saying that the explosions occurred after the Austrians did the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Visible damage may have transpired and passed in six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, with all these provisos, can you assist us further on the question whether, bearing in mind both the photographs and what is in the Austrian investigation report, explosion and damage to surrounding vegetation might have occurred between March and September?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, there's no basis for that question. There's no evidence that there is any damage to vegetation. That's the doctor's point that he testified to. Unless counsel has got something to point to, the Austrians sure don't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, were you listening to what Mr. Hannis said in response, that this damage may have occurred in past, and I prefaced my question by making it clear that subject to all the provisos that have arisen in this discussion, can the witness help us any further. Can you assist us any further, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, something like that is possible; however, what is not possible is for damages on the vegetation to disappear. If bark on the trees was damaged by shrapnel or gun-shots, that could not have disappeared over six months more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, you're not an expert on vegetation, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that as a side finding as I was working with my team on mass graves, the team from my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And trees may have been cut down during the intervening six months, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, let me ask you another question --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not based on the description -- well, yes. At any rate, it is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Another possibility to explain some of these differences is the possibility that the site depicted in the photographs from the Urosevac SUP is not the same site from which the bodies were exhumed by the Austrian forensic team. That's a possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There are many assumptions that can be made, but I wouldn't like to engage in guess-work. I just spoke about the material evidence that I observed and assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that that is a possible explanation because you haven't seen a photograph of the site of the Austrian examination to compare it and determine that it's one and the same place, have you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't see any descriptions to the effect that there were damages on the vegetation or that there were not, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit 6D 501 is the Urosevac report accompanying those photographs that we've been talking about, and page number 2 in the B/C/S -- I don't know if you have a copy of that. We can bring it up for you. Did you have a chance to read that whole report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I just looked at the photo documentation. I did not read the entire report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that page, the second page in B/C/S, describes the case as an act of terrorism in the municipality of Kacanik, the village of Kotlina. And in handwriting is the word "Ivaja," I-v-a-j-a, with a question mark. You don't know who put that on there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to intervene. In the Serbian, there's no question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I withdraw that. That's my mistake. There's a question mark in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Ivaja" is handwritten. You see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And looking at my map of Kosovo and that municipality, it appears there is a village named Ivaja a couple of kilometres south of Kotlina. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Having seen that, does it make it more easy for you to agree with me that the possibility is what's depicted in that Urosevac SUP report is a different site than the one from which the bodies were recovered by the Austrian forensic team? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 29, line 18 today, you were answering a question about whether or not an explosion in the well with these bodies would occur without leaving any biological traces, and you said: "Bearing in mind the depth at which the first mortal remains were found of the bodies that were found in the well, it is impossible to expect in view of the breadth of the well that they could have been ejected out of the well to other areas outside of the well." I know -- I understand your answer that you wouldn't expect it, but you can't tell us with 100 per cent certainty that it's not possible, can you? You've never done any testing for the kind of results that you would get when you had 20 bodies in a well this size and these proportions because you don't know how many and what type of explosives were used and where they were placed, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no one gains experience in that way. I'm speaking on the basis of what can be derived on the basis of the depth and breadth of the well, on the basis of the descriptions of the bodies, and as I mentioned in all these paragraphs. However, had body parts had been ejected from the well into the surrounding area, then that would have to be verified by the investigators in different ways. For example, biological remains that could have been washed away. I'm not challenging that, but then would have to be blood-stains on the charred clothing or parts of tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, you agree with me you're not an expert on explosions and explosives, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for wounds coming from explosives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't know whether there were single or multiple explosions in this case, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or indeed what kind of explosives were used, whether it was a grenade or multiple grenades or a mine or a home-made device. You have no way of knowing that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Investigators found only a few metal parts in the area surrounding the well, which means that grenades, explosive devices, things like that, had that been thrown, the investigators would have found many more metal parts. The only logical conclusion is that there weren't any such explosions in the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, now you're assuming that the investigators made a thorough search for metal parts and used metal detectors, and based on your earlier complaints I'm not sure that you can feel comfortable that they did that, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've just been saying that the investigators worked in a superficial and inadequate way when searching the area of the well and dealing with the victims who were found in these wells.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In -- at page 30, line 22, today you noted the fact that out of one of the wells a bullet was found that was determined to have been made in China in 1964. And you went on to say that this was ammunition used by the Albanians, and they had this ammunition, and its use was recorded in Kosovo, so perhaps it's possible that in an exchange of fire or in a cross-fire of sort a person could have been hit by mistake and then buried in the well. That's a fair bit of speculation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is a fact that implies that the man who had been hit with this Chinese bullet manufactured in 1964 and the members of the police did not have such ammunition and such weapons. When that kind of bullet is found near the body and when it caused an injury, I can base my conclusion on that. That is not speculation. It is based on physical evidence, like the projectile we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me clear that up because I wasn't certain where that came from. Is this bullet an entire unfired bullet, or are you talking about the bullet that has been fired and ejected from its casing and gone through something or at least out of the rifle? Which are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the projectile that was analysed in the laboratory, the ballistics laboratory of the Austrian investigating team. That is on page 101 in Serbian, where reference is made to physical evidence that was found in the well, and then it says: "Bullet found in the dug well, in the wall of the well." Then it says: "Documentation shows that this bullet was made in China and manufactured in 1964."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what material evidence item that is? I wasn't able --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is material evidence 1, material evidence 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. And I see on page 75 of the English that that's described as a 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre with a full-jacket bullet, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: But it also says inter alia on it is a triangular trace of ejection as well as a trace --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said that the MUP didn't have any ammunition like that. Isn't it true that in 1998 and 1999 through Albanian civilians turning in weapons and from the seizure and capture of weapons and ammunition that the MUP in March 1999 had hundreds of such weapons and thousands of rounds of such ammunition? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you read the Austrian report finding about the other bullets and casings that were found during their exhumations, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You make the point that there were only 12 spent shell cases found and in the bodies examined there were at least 26 gun-shot wounds, and from that you get to the conclusion that this was probably a secondary grave-site instead of an execution site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that, I conclude that the gun-shot wounds were sustained elsewhere as far as a number of these bodies are concerned and that after that the bodies were thrown into the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your conclusion is based merely on the absence of a number of shell casings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that there are several other alternative explanations for the absence of additional shell casings, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because some six -- almost six months passed between the time of these alleged killings and the exhumations in September, so some shooters could have carried out shell casings, for example. That's one possibility, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is one of the possibilities, yes, but I don't see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you don't see any reason why? Really?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In an area where tens of thousands of projectiles are spent, if someone has the time to collect casings, then that is another assumption. No one would do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it might be easier than moving the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind the terrain and the circumstances under which the war conflicts in Kosovo took place, I doubt that the people who took part in armed conflicts had enough time for that in view of the possible consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the other hand, if you had managed to disarm a group and line them up and execute them, you might find it advisable to pick up your shell casings to reduce the evidence that might connect you with such an unlawful act, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible in theory, but if one bears in mind the fact that after a round is fired from a handgun, the casings are ejected in a radius of over 10 metres, then it would take a long time to gather all the casings and to remove them; in particular, if we're talking about the circumstances where the terrain is overgrown with deciduous trees and lush vegetation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the things you said at page 35 was that based on the injuries described to the bodies in the well, you did not think that this could have happened from explosions within the well based on the number of such injuries and the location of injuries and the locations of those bodies within the well. Does that allow for the possibility of multiple explosions at different time-periods? For example, five or six bodies were thrown into the well, then there was a grenade tossed in, then other bodies were thrown in, and then there was another grenade. Would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible to throw a couple of bodies and then -- into the well and then to throw an explosive device in and that the injuries would be such that smaller or larger body parts would be destroyed. I said that at the deepest level only body parts were found; in the medium level the bodies were better preserved; whereas on the surface area, again, we encountered extensive destruction to body parts. Some were at the depth of 8 metres; others were found at the depth of 9 metres. So there is a stratum of soil that was a metre deep, and that's virtually impossible. I said that some bodies were found lying prone and there were explosive injuries to the front of the body, and that is impossible. If you throw any explosive device on bodies, it is realistic to expect that any injuries would be to the back because the front of the body was lying against the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to Izbica and your comments on that report. Would you agree with me that many of the wounds that you can see on the dead bodies depicted in that video are consistent with witness accounts that those men were killed by gun-shot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not deny that. I said that where injuries were visible in all those bodies, gun-shot wounds were visible on some or even most of them, and that is not controversial at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things you mentioned -- well, let me ask you this: Did you ever speak or attempt to speak with Dr. Tomasevic about her findings concerning the bodies from Izbica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk to Dr. Tomasevic because she was there in a different capacity. I am not familiar with it. She worked in Kosovo, although nominally I was her chief. But if she accepted to work under those conditions, I had no reason to talk to her. On the other hand, I read a transcript where she told some untruths about me. She said that I was promoted by four ranks after Vukovar. That's a complete fabrication, and I don't want to communicate with people who are able to come up with something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What transcript was that? Not one from this case, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the case -- or rather, I think it is. Yes, I think it is a transcript from this case. Yes, from this case when she spoke about her findings from Izbica where she also made some observations about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I think near the beginning of my questioning of you I asked you if you had read or seen any of the transcripts or videotapes of the testimonies of certain people in this case, including Dr. Tomasevic, and you told me no. But now your memory is that you did see hers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, you did not ask me about Dr. Tomasevic, not a single question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, to assist this is the statement by Dr. Tomasevic, not the transcript, so as to not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it's her statement not her testimony here; is that right, her written statement? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 5 of your comments about Izbica, at the very end you mention: "This video recording does not show grouped bodies, contrary to the statement given by Witness Mustafa Draga: 'The group I was in numbered about 70 men.' Also, in order for him to be protected and shielded from intensive machine-gun and automatic fire, there had to be more bodies around him, as opposed to what the witness said: 'Hajriz fell on top of me... I was saved by Hajriz and God.'" Doctor, that depends on many variables that you simply don't know, right? You don't know how him and Mr. Draga and the other men were lined up, how many gun men were shooting at them, at what angles they fired, how many bullets they fired, how long that lasted, how soon Mr. Draga went to the ground, et cetera. You don't know enough to form that opinion, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I had in mind -- or rather, I took into account Draga Mustafa's statement, and I also took into account what could be seen on the footage. I don't deny that these people are victims, that they are dead, but I could not see anywhere in the statement -- or rather, I could not see the execution site, the 70 bodies that are mentioned in the statement. I saw less people, up to 30, as far as I was able to count in the little forested area and in the meadow in front of it. I didn't see 70 of them. At the same time, next to these people whose bodies had been moved, I did not see any biological traces, blood and so on. I was able to see that they had been moved, and I did not see the number of casings. I'm talking about only this thing, the footage that shows the dead bodies from the point of view of the person recording it, the way he thought that they should be recorded. I have nothing against the footage, but I'm just talking about physical evidence. I'm saying that this was not present at the scene, and this could be seen on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but you're doing more than that. You're challenging Mustafa Draga's account of how he came to survive that shooting when so many others around him were shot and killed, and I'm saying you don't have enough information to dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: If injuries are inflicted by bursts of machine-gun fire and if the bullet causes injury to one body going through that body, it is a certain fact that they would hit another body. If we look at the force of impact of those bullets, during the war we analysed, we looked at the people killed in this manner, people killed when a bullet entered one body, exited, and then entered the other body causing death.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's also one reason why you could have 26 bullet wounds from 14 shell casings, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is impossible to have 84 rounds to cause the death of more than a hundred people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When you have a through-and-through wound, if we were to have the descriptions of injuries as they were done by the Austrians, if they had described them properly, we would have been able to ascertain with a high degree of certainty whether a bullet had passed through the body of one victim and entered the body of another, and that would have been an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But your assumption regarding Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Draga, I'm sorry, Mr. Mustafa Draga, appears to be that he and all 70 men remained standing until they were hit by a bullet and fell down and died. Isn't it possible that Mr. Mustafa managed to fall or dive to the ground before a bullet passed in his direction and passed over him when fired at waist height or higher. That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly, item number 7 and 8, you're talking about Mr. Thaqi's account of what happened with him and the men he was with. And you think his description is impossible, that his jersey and jacket couldn't have gotten bullet-holes in them as he describes. But I think there's a fallacy in your analysis because you seem to read his statement as saying that he noticed the bullet-holes while he was standing up, and that's not what he says. In paragraph 8, you quote him: "Bullets were flying all around me, and some came close to my head, but I wasn't hit. I discovered three bullet-holes in the back of my jacket, my jersey, and also my shirt." So he didn't discover the holes until afterwards. You didn't have a chance to analyse his clothing to see if there were any trace elements of bullet metal on those holes in his jacket or his jersey or his shirt, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, my question is: You didn't have a chance to analyse his clothing for trace elements of bullets?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the footage, yes, because in his statement -- there are actually photographs of the clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So your analysis consists of looking at a photograph of some clothing with what appear to be holes in them; that's the extent of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. In that case, Doctor, I don't have any more questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, yes. I should be able to finish within the time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, first of all I would like to go back to Kotlina. If you can look at 6D 501, pages 11 -- or 10 -- let's go to page 11 in the Serbian since unfortunately the English translation does not have the captions, I don't think, of all the pictures translated. And if we look at -- if we can -- if we could zoom in on the text beneath the first photograph as much as possible, and if the doctor could perhaps read for us if this identifies the location where this is in front of which village. Doctor, are you in a position to be able to read this caption or at least the part that comes after "Selo," or village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Bodies found further up from the village of Kotlina near the second shelter in the form of a well."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, the Prosecutor asked you if, in fact, there was a possibility that this was in Ivaja rather than in Kotlina based upon the handwritten note. Does this picture leave you with the possibility more so than Ivaja that this is actually Kotlina based upon the caption of the photo that you examined?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I always said that wells could be seen at those sites on the photographs. I don't know where in the villages they're located. I'm not familiar with the area, but I can say that on the basis of the documentation, the file, the bodies are located next to the wells.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. The document speaks for the rest of the material contained therein. Mr. Hannis also asked you about body number 8, the one that had little to work with. Does the fact that most of the body of body number 8 in Kotlina, does the fact that most of the body is missing lead you to make any conclusion as to whether, in fact, the well was the locale or the locus of the death or whether that locus was some site elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The description of the body states that only remains of the legs, both feet, and parts of clothing were found. No gun-shot wounds were found, and that meant that most probably the body was destroyed by an explosive device, and that's logical in terms of the explosive wounds and fire marks found on the body. But if this body had been blown apart in the well, then it would be logical to expect that other body parts would be found in the well, the thorax, parts of the skull, the upper limbs, but this is not contained in the description, which means that the injury was caused elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And to clear up one other issue that was raised twice by Mr. Hannis, if you could please enlighten those of us here who are not from the Yugoslav or Serbian legal system, what is the procedure and practice in the Serbian or Yugoslav legal system regarding completing experts in legal cases? Are they to have contact outside of court, such competing experts? According to the ZKP or the Law on Criminal Acts or Criminal Procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, I'm afraid we're going to have to stop for the day at this stage. The case that follows this one is a sensitive one --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and I don't have authority to -- yeah, but your question doesn't really have a foundation because we're not talking about competing experts, are we? We're talking about an expert witness here commenting on the work done by people actively engaged in a job. They're not working as experts when they do that. They're working as pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the Yugoslav system that's covered by ZKP, which is P1824, Articles 250 and 251 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's for tomorrow, I'm afraid, because we just have to stop today, regrettably. I'm sorry about this, Professor, but we have to leave this court to allow another case to take place here this afternoon, and you will have to come back briefly tomorrow morning to complete your evidence. I do deeply regret that, but it's the way things have turned out today because of a lack of focus in the way in which this whole evidence has been presented. As I said before, that does not appear to be your responsibility entirely. So I have to ask you now to leave the courtroom but return to continue your evidence tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of May, 2008, at 9:00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24
